'''''Mesembryanthemum cordifolium''''', formerly known as ''Aptenia cordifolia'', is a [[species]] of [[succulent plant]] in the family [[Aizoaceae]]. It is a creeping plant that forms a carpet of flat-growing [[perennial herb]]s in groups on the ground from a base.<ref>C. Brickell (ed.): Encyclopedia of garden and indoor plants. Orbis, Munich 1994, {{ISBN|3-572-00685-6}}</ref> The [[genus]] name means middle-embryo flower in reference to the position of the ovary in the flower. The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] is derived from [[Latin]] for heart-shaped leaves.<ref name=":0" />

==Description==
This is a succulent, creeping, short-lived, mat-forming perennial [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] growing in flat clumps on the ground from a woody base. Plants only rise to about {{Convert|10|cm|}} tall but prostrate stems reach up to about {{Convert|60|cm|}} long.  The stems are green and stalk-round. The fleshy, small leaves are opposite, [[Ovate (leaf)|ovate]] to [[Cordate (leaf shape)|cordate]], about {{Convert|2.5|cm|}} long and covered with fine [[Plant cuticle|papillae]].

Bright pink to purplish solitary flowers appear in the [[leaf]] [[Axillary bud|axils]], open during the day but close up at night and remain closed on cloudy days. These colored [[Whorl (botany)|whorls]] are not [[petal]]s, but non-functional modified [[stamen]]s. Normal stamens are yellow. Flowers bloom primarily from spring to fall. The fruit is a [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] of little more than one centimeter in length with millimeter brown [[tuberose]] seeds. There is a [[Variegation|variegated]] form.<ref>W. Haage: Cacti and succulents. Quelle & Meyer, Heidelberg 1989, {{ISBN|3-494-01143-5}}</ref>

==Names==
The common names of the plant include '''baby sun rose''',<ref name="PlantzAfrica">{{cite web |url=http://pza.sanbi.org/aptenia-cordifolia |last=Lucas |first=Norma |date=January 2009 |title=Aptenia Cordifolia – PlantZAfrica.com}}</ref> '''heart-leaf''',<ref name=ZAPlantbook>{{cite web |url=http://www.plantbook.co.za/aptenia-cordifolia/ |title=Aptenia Cordifolia – Plantbook}}</ref> '''red aptenia'''<ref name=PlantzAfrica/> or '''aptenia'''<ref name=ZAPlantbook/> in English, as well as '''''rooi brakvygie'''''<ref name=PlantzAfrica/> or '''''brakvygie'''''<ref name=PlantzAfrica/><ref name=ZAPlantbook/> in [[Afrikaans]], and '''''umjuluka''''',<ref name=ZAPlantbook/>{{Disputed inline|Talk page section|for=source possibly mistaken, ''umjuluka'' is word for ''Casearia gladiiformis''|date=August 2019}} '''''ibohlololo''''',<ref name=PlantzAfrica/> or '''''uncolozi omncane'''''<ref name=PlantzAfrica/> in [[isiZulu]] in South Africa. It is known as '''heartleaf iceplant''' in the US<ref>{{PLANTS|id=APCO|taxon=Aptenia cordifolia|accessdate=8 January 2016}}</ref> British names may be '''heart-leaved aptenia'''{{Citation needed|date=August 2019}} or '''heart-leaved midday flower''' because, like many other representatives of the [[Aizoaceae]], it opens its flowers only during the [[sunshine]] of the day.

==Taxonomy==
''Mesembryanthemum cordifolium'' is an accepted name according to "The Plant List"<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2363065|title = Mesembryanthemum cordifolium L.f. — the Plant List}}</ref> database, the primary source for the modern [[Angiosperm Phylogeny Group|APG]] taxonomy of flowering plants. Formerly placed in the genus ''Aptenia'' and known as ''A. cordifolia'', it was included in ''Mesembryanthemum'' in 2007 when the whole genus ''Aptenia'' was reduced to synonymy.<ref>Klak, Cornelia & Bruyns, Peter & Hedderson, Terry. (2007). A Phylogeny and New Classification for Mesembryanthemoideae (Aizoaceae). Taxon. 56. 737-756. 10.2307/25065858.</ref>

Perhaps the most common plant seen under this name in gardens is actually '''''Mesembryanthemum'' 'Red Apple'''', a [[hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] with more vigorous growth, red flowers and bright green leaves, whose parents are ''M. cordifolium'' and ''M. haeckelianum''. The true species of ''M. cordifolium'' has [[magenta]]-[[purple]] flowers and more heart-shaped, mid-green, textured leaves.<ref>Flora of North America Editorial Committee, e. 2003. Magnoliophyta: Caryophyllidae, part 1. 4: i-xxiv, 1-559. In Fl. N. Amer. Oxford University Press, New York</ref><ref>Wunderlin, RP 1998. Guide Vasc. Pl. Florida i-x + 1-806. University Press of Florida, Gainesville</ref>

==Distribution==
Native to the [[Eastern Cape|Eastern Cape Province of South Africa]], this species has become widely known as an [[ornamental plant]]. Today it can be found growing in [[Australia]],<ref>Prescott, A. & J. Venning. 1984. Aizoaceae. Flora of Australia 19-62</ref> [[garden refugee|escaped gardens]] and naturalized in some parts of California, Oregon and Florida, in the Mediterranean region of the Europe and in central Mexico. The plant was recently determined to be invasive in California and was listed as a wildland weed red alert.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=369456&isprofile=0&|title = Mesembryanthemum cordifolium - Plant Finder}}</ref>

==Uses==
The primary use of the plant is ornamental. The locals of the region of origin use the plant for its [[anti-inflammatory]] properties.<ref>J. Ettelt: succulent card index. In: cacti and other succulents. 3/2004.</ref>

''M. cordifolium'' (''A. cordifolia'') contains the [[serotonin reuptake inhibitor]] and [[monoamine releasing agent]] alkaloid [[mesembrine]] and demethylmesembrenol. It was found to contain the second highest levels of mesembrine in an analysis of 21 different plants.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1076/phbi.36.3.173.6350 | title=The Distribution of Mesembrine Alkaloids in Selected Taxa of the Mesembryanthemaceae and their Modification in the Sceletium Derived 'Kougoed' | year=1998 | last1=Smith | first1=Michael T. | last2=Field | first2=Courtney R. | last3=Crouch | first3=Neil R. | last4=Hirst | first4=Manton | journal=Pharmaceutical Biology | volume=36 | issue=3 | pages=173–179 | doi-access= }}</ref> These alkaloids can also be found in Kanna (''[[Sceletium tortuosum]]''). Mesembrine likely plays a dominant role in the antidepressant effects of ''Sceletium tortuosum''.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0378874108004492 | doi=10.1016/j.jep.2008.08.010 | title=Review on plants with CNS-effects used in traditional South African medicine against mental diseases | year=2008 | last1=Stafford | first1=Gary I. | last2=Pedersen | first2=Mikael E. | last3=Van Staden | first3=Johannes | last4=Jäger | first4=Anna K. | journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology | volume=119 | issue=3 | pages=513–537 | pmid=18775771 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Cultivation===
''Mesembryanthemum cordifolium'' can be planted as a fast-growing, not hardy, [[groundcover]] in flower boxes and around traffic lights. The plant needs a sunny spot and well drained soil. This plant is also ideal for covering walls, rockeries and areas bare of grass. Due to its quick growth, it is useful to prevent the growth of [[weed]]s in the field where it is planted. It can also survive without problems in a pot, where it is grown in [[hanging basket]]s so the long trailing branches can hang down with their leaves spaced out. Over-wintering should take place in a frost-free, sunny place at approximately {{Convert|5 to 8|C|}}. No serious insect or disease problems are known. In addition to the species and the hybrid 'Red Apple', one also encounters the variety ''A.'' x. 'Mezoo', a mutant of 'Red Apple' whose variegated leaves have creamy white edges, and rarely on a white-flowering form.

===Propagation===
It easily reproduces from [[cuttings (plants)|cuttings]] of the developed stems, [[root]]s, seeds of its capsular fruit, and even from its own buried leaves. Seeds must be sowed in summer and cuttings can be done in early spring in cooler climates. For cuttings, the plant can be divided and [[Stolon|runners]] can be planted directly into the ground. The garden bed must be readied by digging over the soil. [[Compost]] and a slow-release [[fertilizer]] may be added to ensure healthy growth. With regard to risks, it is very resistant to [[drought]], but with moist soil it grows rapidly. It prefers soil with good [[drainage]]. It cannot withstand [[frost]], where it freezes below {{Convert|-5|C|}}.
